43214.etyen:
Calque of German Wörterbuch (“dictionary”), equivalent to ord (“word”) + bok (“book”), literally “word-book”. The first element is from Old Norse orð (“word”), from Proto-Germanic *wurdą (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom (“word”), from *werh₁- (“to speak, say”). The second element is from Old Norse bók (“book”), from Proto-Germanic *bōks (“letter, written message, book”); its further origin is uncertain.
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk ordbok, Danish ordbog, Swedish ordbok, Icelandic orðabók, Faroese orðabók, German Wörterbuch and Dutch woordenboek (“dictionary”).

1001166.etyen:
Internationalism, based ultimately on Ancient Greek Μᾰκεδονῐ́ᾱ (Măkedonĭ́ā, “Macedonia”); the name was transmitted widely through Latin Macedonia (“Macedonia”) and later European languages. The Ancient Greek name is from Μᾰκεδών (Măkedṓn, “a Macedonian”) and the place-name suffix -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). The ethnonym is traditionally connected with μᾰκεδνός (măkednós, “tall, tapering”); Beekes instead derives this adjective from Pre-Greek, though this analysis has been disputed.
Parallel international forms include Norwegian Nynorsk Makedonia, Danish Makedonien, Swedish Makedonien, German Makedonien, Dutc

1001422.etyen:
Derived from French Rémy, a French short form of Latin Remigius. In Norwegian, Remy is used as a spelling variant of Remi. The Latin name is traditionally derived from rēmex (“oarsman”), genitive rēmigis. Like Remi, it may also be used as a short form of Jeremias. First attested in 1898 in Norway.
Cognate with Danish Remy, Swedish Remy and Finnish Remy.

1002190.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from Italian a due (“for two”). The first element, a (“at, to, for”), is from Latin ad (“to, towards”), from Proto-Italic *ad (“towards”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“to, at”).
The second element, due (“two”), is from Latin duae, the feminine plural of duo (“two”), from Proto-Italic *duō (“two”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ (“two”).

1004750.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse bjarmar (“Bjarmians”), an ethnic name used chiefly in the plural. The Old Norse ethnonym was probably borrowed from Finnic; the exact source form and its original meaning are unknown.
Compare Beormas (“Bjarmians”), the form recorded in the Old English account of Ohthere of Hålogaland's voyage, as well as Norwegian Nynorsk bjarmar, Swedish bjarmer, Danish bjarmer and Icelandic Bjarmar, and the learned Finnish borrowing bjarmi (“Bjarmian”).

1005006.etyen:

The term metaphorically refers to humankind's sinful nature.
